newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian scientists create birth control "pill" for mice.
newsitem.headline: Australian scientists create birth control "pill" for mice.

text.p: Australian scientists, claiming a world-first in pest control, said on Thursday they had created a "mouse pox" that could reduce crop damage by temporarily stopping mice from breeding.

But biocontrol experts at the government's CSIRO scientific research body said the pox and its effects had only been achieved in laboratory experiments and it could be several years before the technique was used to control wild mice.

"We have demonstrated, in the laboratory, that it is technically possible to use a virus to deliver an infertility agent, which will keep mice infertile long enough, we believe, to prevent plagues developing," scientist Lyn Hinds, who developed the virus with colleagues, told Reuters.

The mouse pox used in the experiments was easily manufactured but was not found in wild mice and further research was being conducted on another virus to find a safe way to infect wild mice, she said.
Australian Science Minister Peter McGuaran hailed the CSIRO (Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation) work as a world-first and a humane form of pest control.

"This is the first clear proof that it is possible to use a virus as a 'taxi' to carry immunocontraceptive genes, which induce temporary infertility in mammals by immunising them against their own reproductive protein," he said in a statement.
Hinds' colleague, Ian Ramshaw, said the process worked by injecting a protein normally involved in reproduction into the virus, or mouse pox, and injecting the combination into a laboratory mouse.
The mouse's body, linking the protein with the virus, manufactures anti-bodies to fight the invader. But at the same time, the anti-bodies attack the protein in its own reproductive system.
"It actually prevents the sperm from locking onto the ovum, and makes the mice infertile," Ramshaw told Reuters.
Hinds said more research was needed to ensure the virus did not affect species other than mice or resistant strains of mice.
"It is likely to be 2005 at the earliest before anything is available for use in the field," Hind said.
Parts of Australia are hit by plagues of mice every few years, causing massive damage to grain crops in those areas.
